title: Help Desk Ticket #8675309 - Internet Kiosk Freezing and Lagging
scenario: You are working the Enterprise Help Desk ticket queue and a high-priority ticket has been escalated to you. Ticket #8675309 (opened 5/13/2024, Priority: High, Category: Technical/Bug Reports) reads: "Michael is reporting that the Internet kiosk machine is intermittently freezing and has lagged performance." There are no attachments on the ticket. Using the ticket details, classify the ticket by selecting the appropriate issue, and then select the MOST likely root cause of that issue.

rows.prompt: #8675309 - "Michael is reporting that the Internet kiosk machine is intermittently freezing and has lagged performance."

explanation: The two words that decide this ticket are "intermittently freezing" and "lagged performance." A machine that locks up in bursts and then recovers is being starved of processor time by something that runs periodically, not something that is continuously consuming a fixed resource - so the issue is High CPU Utilization rather than High Memory Utilization, which produces steady, worsening sluggishness and paging rather than an on-again/off-again freeze. Of the processes offered in the "Caused by" list, wuauclt.exe is the Windows Update Client: it wakes on a schedule to scan for, download, and install updates, and while it does so it can drive CPU to 90-100% and stall everything else on the box until the scan completes. That periodic wake-and-spike behavior maps exactly to the reported symptom pattern, and it is especially disruptive on a low-spec, always-on Internet kiosk that is rarely rebooted and therefore accumulates a large backlog of pending updates. The distractors are there to test process knowledge: svchost.exe is a generic service host, taskmgr.exe and notepad.exe are trivial consumers, "User" and "Asset Tag" are not processes at all, and Chrome.exe/Firefox.exe are both offered precisely so that neither browser can be singled out as the culprit from the ticket text alone. As an analyst, the follow-up step is to confirm in Task Manager or with Get-Process that the CPU spikes correlate in time with wuauclt.exe activity before recommending a change to the update window.
confidenceNote: The second exhibit (q259_p435_X10111.png.png) explicitly red-boxes "High CPU Utilization" and "wuauclt.exe" as the key, which is the strongest evidence available, but the community discussion is genuinely split - several commenters argue for High Memory Utilization + Chrome.exe on a kiosk, and multiple real test-takers report the live exam randomizes the process data (one reported notepad.exe with maxed memory), so the reasoning is sound for this exhibit but the exact pairing may vary by exam form.

title: Phishing Kill Chain: Choosing a Control for Each Stage
scenario: A company recently suffered a security incident. A phishing email was delivered to the entire organization; one user clicked a link embedded in the message, which caused a malware executable to be downloaded, installed, executed, and ultimately used to encrypt files on the host. During the post-incident review you have the incident artifacts available (firewall log, file integrity monitoring report, malware domain list, vulnerability scan report, and the phishing email itself) and you must walk the attack backwards along its kill chain. For each stage of the kill chain listed below, select the single security control that would have broken the chain at that point and improved the organization's security posture. Each control may only be used once, and not all of the controls offered will be used.

rows.prompt: Phishing email - the crafted message is delivered to the mailboxes of the entire company
Active links - the message body contains a live, clickable hyperlink pointing to the attacker's site
Malicious website access - the user's browser reaches out and connects to the attacker-controlled host
Malware download - the malicious executable is pulled across the perimeter into the organization
Malware install - the downloaded file is installed onto the endpoint
Malware execution - the installed malware runs on the compromised host
File encryption - the malware encrypts the victim's files (ransomware payload)

explanation: Each control has to break the one specific link it is paired with, and because a control may be used only once the seven picks must be mutually exclusive. Email filtering stops the phishing message at the gateway before any user sees it; forcing mail to render in plain text strips the HTML so the embedded link is no longer active or clickable; an IP blocklist denies the outbound connection to the attacker-controlled host; a firewall file type filter blocks the executable from ever crossing the perimeter; restricted local user permissions prevent a standard user from installing the binary; updated antivirus detects the known-bad file at execution; and backups are the only listed control that actually lets you recover from ransomware encryption. Watch the two strongest distractors in the exhibit's dropdown: disk-level encryption protects data at rest against a stolen drive and does nothing against ransomware (which encrypts files the logged-in user can already read), and VPN only tunnels traffic - it does not neutralize an active link in an email. Honeypot, MAC filtering, MFA, network segmentation and VPN are the controls left unused, which matches the instruction that not all controls will be used. For Part 1 of this simulation, the 'Identify the following' panel offers four files, seven IP addresses and seven timestamps: Invoice.exe is the only executable in the list and is the one consistent with malware that was downloaded, installed and run (an .xlsx cannot carry a macro payload - .xlsm can), the malicious IP seen in the firewall log is 81.161.63.253 with 81.161.63.103 as a near-identical decoy, and the malware entered the organization at 1 Dec 2019 14:03:19.
confidenceNote: Six of the seven kill chain mappings are agreed on by essentially every commenter and by the marked-up screenshot, but that screenshot's hand-drawn answer key picks VPN for 'Active links' where the highest-voted community answers (and the technical logic) say plain text email format, and it also claims payroll.xlsx / 81.161.63.103 for Part 1 while the top-voted commenter who read the firewall log reports Invoice.exe and an IP ending in .253.

title: Distribution Center Hardening Review: Discover Devices, Roles, and Non-Compliant Services
scenario: You are a penetration tester reviewing the system hardening guidelines for a company's distribution center. The guidelines require that (1) there is exactly one primary server or service per device, (2) only default ports are used, (3) non-secure protocols are disabled, and (4) the corporate Internet presence sits in a protected subnet. The network diagram shows four hosts on the internal LAN - CandyManCarl.Local, FarmerLaura.Local, SandwichSara.Local, and FarmerTed.Local - all connected back to the console, plus LunchTimeMike.Local sitting inside a DMZ behind the firewall that faces the Internet. Host and service discovery scans (nmap) run from the console found five live hosts using these addresses, listed here in no particular order: 192.168.1.10, 192.168.1.20, 192.168.1.30, 192.168.1.40, and 10.10.10.25. For each device, record its IP address, choose the primary server or service it provides, and choose the one running service that violates the hardening guidelines and must therefore be disabled.

rows.prompt: CandyManCarl.Local - host on the internal LAN
FarmerLaura.Local - host on the internal LAN
SandwichSara.Local - host on the internal LAN
FarmerTed.Local - host on the internal LAN, directly attached to the console segment
LunchTimeMike.Local - host inside the DMZ, behind the firewall facing the Internet

explanation: Each device is scanned with nmap from the console, and its primary role is the one production service it listens for on a default port: CandyManCarl.Local serves files (SMB/CIFS 445), FarmerLaura.Local handles mail (SMTP 25 / IMAP/S 993), SandwichSara.Local runs the database (MYSQL 3306), FarmerTed.Local is the switch that the other internal hosts hang off of in the diagram, and LunchTimeMike.Local is the only system in the DMZ, so it is the corporate Internet presence - the web server - which is why it is on a separate protected subnet (10.10.10.25) instead of the internal 192.168.1.0/24 range. The non-compliant entry for each device is the leftover service that breaks one of the four guidelines. FTP 21 on the file server, IMAP 143 on the mail server, Telnet 23 on the switch, and HTTP 80 on the DMZ web server are all cleartext protocols that have secure equivalents already available (SMB/CIFS 445, IMAP/S 993, SSH 22, and HTTPS 443 respectively), so they violate the "non-secure protocols should be disabled" rule. DNS 53 on SandwichSara.Local is different: it is a second, unrelated server role running on a box whose primary service is the database, so it breaks the "one primary server or service per device" rule and also widens the attack surface for DNS-based tunneling and exfiltration. Note that the pick is always the insecure or extra service, never the device's own primary service - disabling SMB/CIFS on a file server or HTTPS on a web server would break the system's stated purpose.
confidenceNote: The exhibit marks no selections, so the key comes from the highest-voted community answer (13 upvotes) whose role and protocol choices are internally consistent with all four hardening guidelines; the second image, which is an unsourced answer write-up, was rejected because it lists many protocols per single-select dropdown, labels three different hosts as Web Server (breaking the one-service-per-device rule), and invents sequential IPs, and at least one commenter disputed its accuracy.

title: Website Defacement: Identify the Source IP, IoC, and Corrective Actions
scenario: An organization's public website (https://mycompany.com) was maliciously altered. Three sources of evidence were collected from the web server covering 2022-04-01 and 2022-04-02 and are shown in the exhibits: (1) the SFTP server log, which records logins, logouts, directory changes and file writes along with the client IP and username; (2) the output of 'netstat -ano' on the web server, showing current TCP connections and their states; and (3) the HTTP access log, showing which clients requested pages from the site. All SFTP activity in the log was performed with the single account 'sjames'. Using the three exhibits together, determine which source IP address the analyst should be most concerned about, identify the indicator of compromise, and choose the TWO appropriate corrective actions.

columns.label: Which source IP address should the analyst be most concerned about:
Corrective action (1 of 2):
options: Change the password on the sjames account.
Shut down the insecure file transfer server.

columns.label: Corrective action (2 of 2):
options: Change the password on the sjames account.
Shut down the insecure file transfer server.

rows.prompt: Website defacement findings

action1: Change the password on the sjames account.

explanation: Correlate the three tabs against the actual complaint, which is that the website was altered. In the SFTP log the external address 41.21.18.102 logs in as sjames at 23:01:50, changes to /var/www at 23:01:54, writes './index.html' at 23:02:25 (the site's home page), and logs out at 23:03:18; the HTTP access log then shows 41.21.18.102 issuing a GET for https://mycompany.com at 23:02:56, the attacker verifying its own defacement, and 'netstat -ano' shows 127.0.0.1:38666 to 41.21.18.102:22 still ESTABLISHED, meaning that session is live on the server. The indicator of compromise is therefore the modified index.html file, since that single write is what changed the site; the earlier './index written' and './about_us.html written' entries came from internal 192.168.x addresses during normal business hours. The correct corrective actions are to change the password on the sjames account, because that one credential is clearly compromised and was used from a foreign public IP, and to block external SFTP access, because exposing SFTP to the Internet is the actual attack path. Deleting the account or shutting the file transfer server down entirely would break legitimate internal publishing, encrypting index.html does nothing to stop an authenticated write, and denying 192.168.*.* would block only the organization's own internal network. Note that 32.111.16.37 is a decoy: it produced one 10-second session with no file activity, a single failed login, and three already-closed (TIME_WAIT) connections, so it is suspicious but never touched a file.
confidenceNote: Exhibit q332_p530_X11598.png.png is a marked-up answer key asserting the source IP is 32.111.16.37 because of 'repeated failed login attempts', but the SFTP log contains only ONE failed login from that address and no file writes at all, so that rationale is directly contradicted by the evidence; every substantive commenter (TommyZ, Popeyes_Chicken, 7167087, taketaa - the three highest-voted posts in the discussion) independently concludes 41.21.18.102, the address that actually wrote index.html and still holds an ESTABLISHED connection, which is what I used, while the IoC and both corrective actions are agreed on by the answer key and the community alike.

title: Data Exfiltration Triage: Command Identification and Tampered Binary
scenario: An organization has noticed large amounts of data being sent out of its network, and you are the analyst assigned to find the cause. Four tabs of collected evidence from the suspect Windows host (192.168.10.21) are available: Tab 1 is a console listing of active TCP connections showing the protocol, local address, foreign address, connection state, PID and the owning executable in brackets. Tab 2 is a console listing of running processes showing image name, PID, session name, session number and memory usage. Tab 3 is the output of `Get-ChildItem | Get-FileHash -Algorithm MD5`, giving the current MD5 hash of each file on the host. Tab 4 lists the organization's known-good baseline MD5 hash signatures for those same files. Using this evidence, determine which command produced the Tab 1 output, which command produced the Tab 2 output, and which file is responsible for the malicious behavior.

columns.label: Command that generated the output in Tab 1
Command that generated the output in Tab 2
File responsible for the malicious behavior

rows.prompt: Exfiltration analysis of host 192.168.10.21

explanation: Tab 1's columns (Proto, Local address, Foreign address, State, PID) with the owning executable printed in brackets under each entry are exactly what `netstat -bo` produces: -b names the executable that owns the connection and -o adds the PID; plain netstat, arp -a and nslookup do not show PIDs or binaries. Tab 2's columns (Image Name, PID, Session Name, Session#, Mem Usage) are the standard `tasklist` output. For the malicious file, compare Tab 3 (current hashes) against Tab 4 (baseline): explorer.exe, svchost.exe and, importantly, sftp.exe (10ad132ffed0217c6c3854a22bab215c6) all match their baselines, so sftp.exe is an unmodified legitimate binary even though it holds SSH sessions. cmd.exe, by contrast, hashes to 372ab227fd5ea779c211a1451881d1e1 against a baseline of a2cdef1c445d3890cc3456789058cd21 - it has been replaced or tampered with - and Tab 1 shows that same cmd.exe (PID 3467) holding an ESTABLISHED HTTPS session out to the public address 31.10.100.7, while Tab 2 shows Cmd.exe at 18,020 K of memory, orders of magnitude more than every other process. A modified system binary that is beaconing outbound over 443 and consuming abnormal memory is the exfiltration vector; the changed hashes on the data files users.txt and calendar.dat are the data that was staged and altered, not the mechanism.
confidenceNote: The netstat -bo and tasklist answers are unambiguous from the output column headers, and cmd.exe is confirmed by a decisive hash mismatch against baseline plus an outbound HTTPS connection and 18,020 K memory usage - one commenter argued for sftp.exe, but sftp.exe's hash matches the baseline exactly, and the source material's own answer-key page states cmd.exe.

title: Prioritizing Vulnerability Remediation Against an SLA Standard
scenario: A systems administrator is reviewing the output of a vulnerability scan. Three sources of information are shown below: (1) the scan output listing each finding with its affected asset, risk and CVE/CVSS reference; (2) the environment architecture table, which maps each subnet to an environment (prod.comptia.org, dev.comptia.org, uat.comptia.org), shows whether it is internet-facing, and lists the controls in place (NGFW, load balancer, MFA); and (3) the organization's vulnerability remediation timeframe standard, which sets a patching SLA per CVSS band and states which environments each SLA applies to. Using the environment architecture and the remediation standard, identify the server that must be patched within 14 calendar days, and select the appropriate technique and mitigation for the vulnerability on that server.

columns.label: Select the server to be patched within 14 calendar days
Select the appropriate technique and mitigation
options: Patch; issue a CRL for the server to the CA
Patch; upload signed certificate from trusted third-party provider
Compensating control; implement MFA on the application
Patch; upgrade IIS to current release
Request exception; legacy protocol could have operational impact
Compensating control; implement secure session tokens
Compensating control; create new ACL on firewall to block port 443
Request exception; organization needs time to procure a PKI

rows.prompt: The one finding in the scan output that falls under the 14-calendar-day remediation SLA, and how it should be remediated

answer.mitigation: Patch; upload signed certificate from trusted third-party provider

explanation: The remediation standard assigns the 14-calendar-day SLA only to the CVSS > 7.9 < 9.0 band, and the 'Applies to' columns show that band is checked for PROD but marked with a red X for UAT and DEV. Only three findings land in that band, all CVSS 8.1 'Untrusted SSL/TLS Server X.509 certificate' (CVE-2021-1234) on 192.168.76.5, 192.168.50.5 and 192.168.60.5. The environment table places 192.168.76.0/24 in dev.comptia.org and 192.168.50.0/24 in uat.comptia.org, so neither of those is covered by the 14-day requirement; 192.168.60.0/24 belongs to prod.comptia.org, which is externally hosted and publicly accessible, making 192.168.60.5 the only server in scope. Because the finding is that the server's certificate is signed by an untrusted or unknown CA (risk: an on-path attacker could insert a spoofed certificate for any DN), the fix must replace the certificate itself: patch the server by uploading a signed certificate from a trusted third-party provider. The distractors do not remediate the root cause: the CVSS 9.2 IIS finding ('Patch; upgrade IIS to current release') is on the dev host 192.168.76.5 where no SLA applies, MFA and secure session tokens address the missing-authentication and insecure-cookie findings, blocking port 443 with an ACL would break the service rather than fix the trust chain, and a CRL revokes a certificate without issuing a trusted replacement. Exceptions and compensating controls are only appropriate when a patch is unavailable, which is not the case here.
confidenceNote: The excluded exhibit q413_p628_X13003.png.png is a marked-up answer key showing green boxes around the 192.168.60.5 checkbox and the 'Patch; upload signed certificate from trusted third-party provider' option, and both community commenters independently derive the same answer from the CVSS band, the PROD-only applicability of the 14-day SLA, and the subnet-to-environment mapping.

title: Risk Assessment Action Plan: Categorize and Prioritize Findings
scenario:
A healthcare organization must build an action plan from the findings of a risk assessment. The action plan consists of two parts: categorizing each risk and setting the order in which the findings will be remediated.

Two reference documents are shown below. The Risk audit report lists eight findings, each with a Likelihood of occurrence value (1-5) and a Severity of impact value (1-5). The Risk matrix converts those two values into a risk rating score (Likelihood x Severity) and shows the score for every combination.

For each finding in the table, calculate its risk rating score, assign the matching risk categorization, and assign a prioritization number from 1 (remediate first) to 8 (remediate last) based on that score. Each prioritization number is used exactly once.

rows.prompt: A list of patient prescription information was emailed to the incorrect recipient.
Improperly configured third-party websites pose security risks to internal assets.
A large volume of ICMP traffic is detected from an external source to Server2.
Unauthorized software was discovered on technician workstations.
The internet-facing web server allows access to data without requiring credentials.
A large number of potentially malicious emails is reaching end-user and shared mailboxes.
PHI data was found within the development and test environments.
Sensitive materials were found on a fax machine in a common area.

explanation: This PBQ is pure risk-matrix arithmetic: the score is Likelihood of occurrence multiplied by Severity of impact, and the matrix bands it as Low (0-4), Medium (5-9), or High (10-25). Reading the likelihood/severity pairs out of the audit report gives: malicious emails 5x5=25 High, ICMP flood at Server2 5x4=20 High, prescription PHI emailed to the wrong recipient 3x5=15 High, PHI in dev/test 3x3=9 Medium, fax machine documents 3x2=6 Medium, unauthorized software 2x2=4 Low, internet-facing web server 3x1=3 Low, and third-party certificate issues 2x1=2 Low. Prioritization is simply that score list sorted from highest to lowest, so 25 is priority 1 and 2 is priority 8. Note the traps built into the descriptions: the fax machine and misdirected prescription findings both involve PHI, but severity is not automatically Critical - the fax documents rate only Minor impact (2), while the misdirected email of 15 patients' prescriptions rates Critical (5). Likewise the unauthenticated web server sounds alarming, but the report states its data is marketing material that is required to be publicly available, so impact is Negligible (1) and it lands near the bottom of the queue. Always let the assessed likelihood and impact values drive the ranking rather than how frightening a finding's title sounds.
confidenceNote: The likelihood x severity math from the audit report and risk matrix is unambiguous and exactly matches the answer both discussion commenters converged on; the fourth image's green-highlighted key is demonstrably self-contradictory (it tags the fax finding, score 6, as Low and the unauthorized-software finding, score 4, as Medium, and leaves the web-server row unmarked), so it was treated as an unreliable markup rather than ground truth.

title: Phishing Incident Scoping: Clicks, Infections and the Dropper
scenario: It is 3/7/2016 at AnyCorp. Approximately 100 employees have received a phishing email, and you are the security analyst assigned to scope the incident. Three log sources are shown below. The Email Server log records message delivery (date/time, source IP, source port, From and To). The File Server log is the outbound web proxy record for the 192.168.0.0/24 workstation subnet (date/time, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, URL and HTTP method). The SIEM log holds Windows security events from those workstations — 4624 Logon, 4634 Logoff, 4688 Process Creation and 4689 Process Termination — with the workstation IP address, account name, process ID and process name. Correlate the three logs and answer: how many employees actually clicked the link in the phishing email, on how many workstations was the malware actually installed, and what is the file name of the malicious executable?

columns.label: Your answer
columns.placeholder: a number, or a file name

rows.prompt: How many employees clicked on the link in the phishing email?
On how many workstations was the malware installed?
What is the executable file name of the malware?

explanation: The Email Server log shows the phishing wave arriving from it-helpdesk@sobergrill.com at external IP 58.125.17.196 (source port 54566) between 4:00:00 PM and 4:01:37 PM, addressed to roughly 100 anycorp.com users — that is delivery, not clicks, so it is not the number you report. In the web proxy (File Server) log every domain resolves to a different destination IP on each request except chzweb.tilapia.com, which is always 33.225.130.104; that constant callback host is the link in the email, and exactly seven distinct workstations request it after the mail lands: 192.168.0.132 (4:01:34 PM), .134 (4:04:21), .254 (4:05:14), .24 (4:08:45), .9 (4:10:16), .70 (4:11:34) and .188 (4:14:04). Clicking is not the same as compromise: in the SIEM, Event ID 4688 Process Creation for mailclient.exe fires exactly 30 seconds after the GET on only four of those seven hosts — 192.168.0.132/asmith at 4:02:04, 192.168.0.24/jlee at 4:09:15, 192.168.0.9/lbalk at 4:10:46 and 192.168.0.188/kmatthews at 4:14:34 — so four workstations were infected and three clickers were not (they were likely blocked or patched). Every other process name offered is either a normal Windows/Office/browser binary or, like time.exe at 4:00:26 PM on 192.168.0.141, appears only as a 4689 process-termination event on a host that never made a web request at all, so it cannot be the dropper. The technique to carry into the exam: pivot email → URL → process creation, anchor on the constant destination IP to find the malicious link, and count distinct hosts at each stage rather than raw log lines.
confidenceNote: The log evidence is internally airtight — seven hosts hit the one URL with a constant destination IP, and mailclient.exe is created via Event ID 4688 exactly 30 seconds after the GET on four of them — but one source screenshot is marked in green with 4 / 1 / time.exe, and those values cannot be reproduced from the exhibits (192.168.0.141, the only time.exe host, never appears in the web logs at all, and its event is a process termination, not a creation), while the community discussion itself is contradictory (one poster said 20 clicks / 8 workstations / putty.exe, another said 11 clicks, and a poster who sat the live exam chose mailclient.exe).
